Is cannabis an aphrodisiac?

By HowToEdibles Editorial Team March 5, 2026 6 min read

Explore the relationship between cannabis and sexual desire. Learn how THC and CBD may enhance intimacy, arousal, and pleasure.

Home / Articles / Is Cannabis an Aphrodisiac?

Short answer

Not reliably, though many users say it helps. In a 2019 survey of 216 people who used cannabis with sex, 59% said it increased desire and 74% said it increased satisfaction, and a study of more than 51,000 U.S. adults linked cannabis use with more frequent sex. These are self-reported surveys that can't prove cause and effect, and higher doses can cause anxiety, sedation or trouble with arousal.

Not medical advice

This article is general education, not medical advice. If you have ongoing problems with desire, arousal, or pain during sex, or take prescription medications, talk to a doctor before using cannabis. Cannabis can impair judgment — only have sex when everyone involved can clearly consent.

Table of Contents

Cannabis has been used as an aphrodisiac for thousands of years. Ancient Indian Ayurvedic texts describe cannabis preparations called "bhang" as enhancers of sexual pleasure. Today, modern research is beginning to test these traditional claims.

What the research says

A 2017 study published in the Journal of Sexual Medicine analyzed survey data from more than 51,000 U.S. adults and found that cannabis users reported having significantly more sex than people who had never used it. While frequency alone does not prove enhanced desire, other surveys have found that a majority of cannabis users report that it improves their sexual experiences. In a 2019 online survey of 216 people, 59% said cannabis increased their desire, 74% reported more satisfaction, and 66% reported more intense orgasms. A 2019 survey of 373 women at a U.S. clinic found that those who used cannabis before sex had about twice the odds of reporting satisfactory orgasms. All of these studies rely on self-reports from people who already use cannabis, so they show associations, not cause and effect.

The endocannabinoid system, which THC and CBD interact with, plays a role in regulating mood, pleasure, and stress — all factors that directly influence sexual desire and performance. When cannabinoids activate receptors in the brain associated with pleasure and reward, the result can be heightened sensitivity and a deeper sense of connection.

How cannabis enhances intimacy

Reduced anxiety and inhibition. One of the most common barriers to sexual enjoyment is stress and anxiety. Cannabis, particularly strains high in CBD or balanced THC:CBD ratios, can quiet a racing mind and help people feel more present and relaxed during intimate moments.

Heightened sensory perception. THC is known to enhance sensory experiences — colors look brighter, music sounds richer, and touch feels more intense. This amplification of touch and sensation can make physical intimacy feel more pleasurable and immersive.

Altered perception of time. Many cannabis users report that time seems to slow down, which can make intimate moments feel longer and more enjoyable. What might feel like a brief encounter can take on a quality of timelessness.

The dose makes the difference

Here is where it gets nuanced. Low to moderate doses of cannabis tend to enhance sexual desire and pleasure, while high doses can have the opposite effect — causing sedation, anxiety, or difficulty with arousal. The key is finding your sweet spot.

No dose has been tested in clinical trials for sex, so follow general edible guidance: start with about 2.5 mg of THC (no more than 5 mg if you're new or sensitive), and wait at least 2 hours before taking more. Edibles come on slowly and last for hours, so try a dose on your own first to learn how it affects you, and plan your timing ahead. Don't combine cannabis with alcohol or other drugs, and talk to a doctor first if you take prescription medications.

Cannabis topicals for intimacy

Cannabis-infused lubricants and massage oils have become increasingly popular, and some users report enhanced arousal and more intense orgasms. However, no clinical trials have tested these products, and claims that topical THC increases blood flow to erogenous zones are unproven. Many of these products are oil-based (often coconut oil), and the CDC warns that oil-based products can cause condoms to break — so don't use them with condoms. Test a small amount on your skin first, since oils and additives can irritate sensitive areas.

Strain matters

Not all cannabis is created equal when it comes to setting the mood. Strains high in the terpene limonene tend to be uplifting and mood-enhancing, while strains rich in linalool promote relaxation. Heavy indica strains with high myrcene content might be too sedating. A balanced hybrid or a sativa-leaning strain is generally recommended for intimate occasions.

The bottom line

Cannabis is not a guaranteed aphrodisiac — individual responses vary widely based on dose, strain, tolerance, and personal chemistry. But for many people, a low dose of cannabis can reduce anxiety, heighten physical sensation, and create a deeper sense of connection during intimate moments. As with all cannabis use, the key is moderation: start low, go slow, and find what works for you.

Sources

  1. Sun AJ, Eisenberg ML. "Association Between Marijuana Use and Sexual Frequency in the United States: A Population-Based Study." The Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2017. doi:10.1016/j.jsxm.2017.09.005
  2. Wiebe E, Just A. "How Cannabis Alters Sexual Experience: A Survey of Men and Women." The Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2019. doi:10.1016/j.jsxm.2019.07.023
  3. Lynn BK, et al. "The Relationship between Marijuana Use Prior to Sex and Sexual Function in Women." Sexual Medicine, 2019. PMC6522945
  4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "How to Use a Condom." CDC. cdc.gov
